intro: Every group needs a way to get along. A family does. A class does. A city and a country do too. In this unit, you will learn about rules, fairness and leaders.
You will see why we have rules at home, at school and on the road. You will learn what makes a rule fair. You will meet leaders like mayors, governors, presidents, kings and emperors.
By the end, you will be able to say why rules help us. You will know how a vote works. You will know ways to take turns, share and be kind to everyone.
bigQuestion: How do rules, fairness and leaders help people live and work together?

timeline.t: A group has a problem, like a game that stops working.
Everyone talks and listens to each idea.
The group makes one fair rule for everyone.
If someone breaks it, they say sorry and try again.
The group votes to choose, and the most votes win.
A leader helps the group work together.
Everyone takes turns, shares and helps.

words.d: words that tell us what to do or not do
the same for everyone, with nobody left out
a rule for everyone in a town, state or country
what happens after we do something
a person who helps a group work together
the leader of a city or town
a way each person shows their choice
treating someone as important and caring how they feel

choices: To keep us safe and be fair
test.why: Rules keep us safe and help us be fair.
Stopping at a red light is a road rule.
A fair rule is the same for everyone.

choices: A rule for a whole town, state or country
test.why: A law is a rule for everyone in a town, state or country.

test.q: You break a rule by mistake. What helps?
test.why: We say sorry, fix it and try again.
The president leads the United States.

test.q: Who is the king of the United Kingdom?
test.why: King Charles III is the king of the United Kingdom.

test.q: In a vote, which choice wins?
choices: The one with the most votes
The one with the fewest votes
test.why: The choice with the most votes wins.

test.q: A new child speaks a different language. What is kind?
test.why: Being kind helps others feel welcome. Different is just different.

write.prompt: Should your class vote on the next class game, or should the teacher pick? Say what you think. Use two things you learned in this unit to explain why.
tips: Use a word from the unit, like fair or vote.
Tell one reason from a story or lesson.
Say one good thing about the other idea too.

title: Rules, Fairness and Leaders

chapters.title: Why We Have Rules
chapters.bigQuestion: How do rules help us stay safe and be fair to each other?

story.title: The Game That Fell Apart
story.kicker: A tag game stops working. Then the children make one rule together.
paragraphs: It is recess at a school in Chicago. Six children play tag. Maya is it. She runs and tags Omar. Omar says, "No! I was on the slide. The slide is safe!"
Maya frowns. "Nobody said the slide was safe." Now Lin says the tree is safe too. Ben says his shoe was untied, so it does not count. Everyone talks at once. Nobody is running now.
The game has stopped. Omar sits on the grass. Maya sits too. "This is not fun," says Lin. Ben nods. Then Maya has an idea. "Let's pick one rule. We all use the same one."
They talk. They agree: only the big tree is safe, and only for a count of five. Everyone says yes. Maya counts, "Ready, go!" The game starts again. This time, it works.
story.think: Why did the game start again after the children agreed on one rule?

lessons.title: Rules at Home
lessons.mainIdea: Families make rules to keep everyone safe and happy at home.
reading: Sofia comes home from school. She puts her shoes by the door. She washes her hands. Then she eats a snack. These are her family's rules.
A *rule* tells us what to do or what not to do. Families make rules. Grown-ups often make them. Kids can help too. Each family has its own rules.
Some home rules keep us safe. Do not touch the hot stove. Some rules help us get along. Take turns with the toys. Rules help a home feel calm.

words.d: words that tell us what to do or not do

look.title: Bedtime at Kenji's House
look.text: Look at Kenji's house at night. The clock says 8. Kenji brushes his teeth. He puts on his pajamas. His dad reads one book. Then the light goes off. Kenji knows these steps every night.
look.prompt: What rules does Kenji's family have at bedtime? What is one rule at your home?

check.q: What does a rule tell us?
choices: What to do or not do
check.why: A rule tells us what to do or what not to do.

check.q: Which rule keeps a child safe at home?
choices: Do not touch the hot stove
check.why: A hot stove can burn you. The rule keeps you safe.

check.q: Do all families have the same rules?
choices: Yes, every family is the same
No, each family has its own rules
check.why: The reading says each family has its own rules.

lessons.title: Rules at School
lessons.mainIdea: School rules help everyone learn, play and stay safe.
reading: It is morning in Room 12. Children raise their hands to talk. They walk in the hall. They line up for lunch. Everyone knows what to do.
Rules help a class work well. When one person talks at a time, all can hear. When we walk inside, nobody falls. Rules help us learn and play.

words.d: a group of children who learn together

look.title: Two Kinds of Circle Time
look.text: Picture circle time. First, everyone talks at once. It is loud. Nobody can hear the story. Now picture it again. Each child raises a hand. One child talks. Everyone hears.
look.prompt: Which circle time works better? Which rule helped?

check.q: Why do children raise their hands to talk?
choices: So one person talks at a time
check.why: When one person talks at a time, everyone can hear.

check.q: Why do we walk in the hall?
check.why: Walking inside keeps children from falling.

check.q: What do school rules help us do?
check.why: The reading says rules help us learn and play.

lessons.title: Rules on the Road
lessons.mainIdea: Road rules keep people safe when they walk, ride and drive.
reading: Ana and her mom stand at the corner. The light is red. Cars zoom by. They wait. The walk sign lights up. Now they cross.
Roads have rules too. Red means stop. Green means go. Walkers use the crosswalk. Riders wear helmets. These rules help keep everyone safe.
Drivers follow the rules. Walkers follow the rules. When everyone does, people get where they are going safely.

words.d: the marked place where people cross a street
kept away from getting hurt

look.title: At the Stoplight
look.text: Look at the street corner. A red light glows. A bus stops. A boy on a bike stops too. He wears a blue helmet. Then the light turns green. The bus goes. The boy rides on.
look.prompt: What rules do you see people following at this corner?

check.q: What does a red light mean?
check.why: Red means stop. Green means go.

check.q: Where should walkers cross the street?
check.why: Walkers use the crosswalk. Drivers look for people there.

check.q: Why do bike riders wear helmets?
check.why: Helmets are a road rule that keeps riders safe.

lessons.title: The Same Rule for All
lessons.mainIdea: A fair rule is the same for everyone.
reading: The class plays a game. The rule is: wait for your turn. Leo waits. Pia waits. Then the teacher's helper wants to skip ahead. "The rule is for me too," she says. She waits.
A rule is *fair* when it is the same for everyone. Big kids and little kids. New kids and old friends. Nobody gets to skip the rule. That is how we trust it.

words.d: the same for everyone, with nobody left out

look.title: Who Gets the Swing?
look.text: Look at the swings. Three children want one swing. One girl says, "I am the oldest. I go all day!" Another girl says, "Let's each swing for a count of twenty." Everyone gets a turn.

check.q: When is a rule fair?
choices: When it is the same for everyone
When only big kids use it
check.why: A fair rule is the same for everyone.

check.q: Why did the helper wait her turn?
choices: She did not like the game
The rule was for her too
check.why: She said the rule was for her too. Fair rules are for everyone.

check.q: In the swing picture, which idea is fair?
choices: Each child swings for a count of twenty
check.why: Each child gets the same turn. That is fair.

lessons.title: Oops! Fix It and Try Again
lessons.mainIdea: When a rule is broken, we fix it and try again.
reading: Jamal runs in the hall. He bumps into Rosa. Her books fall. Jamal stops. He says, "I am sorry." He helps pick up the books.
Everyone breaks a rule sometimes. That is how we learn. We can say sorry. We can help fix what went wrong. Then we try again.
Sometimes there is a *consequence*. That is what happens after we do something. Jamal walks back and walks again. Next time, he remembers to walk.

words.d: what happens after we do something
a word we say when we know we hurt someone

look.title: The Spilled Paint
look.text: Look at the art table. Grace grabs the paint too fast. Blue paint spills on Tom's picture. Tom looks sad. Grace gets a paper towel. She says sorry. She helps Tom start a new picture.
look.prompt: How did Grace fix what went wrong?

check.q: What can you do after you break a rule?
choices: Say sorry and help fix it
check.why: We can say sorry, help fix it and try again.

check.q: What is a consequence?
choices: What happens after we do something
check.why: A consequence is what happens after we do something.

check.q: What did Jamal do after he bumped Rosa?
choices: He helped pick up her books
check.why: Jamal said sorry and helped pick up the books.

lessons.title: Laws Are Rules for a Country
lessons.mainIdea: Laws are rules for a whole town, state or country.
reading: A family drives in the car. Everyone wears a seat belt. The baby sits in a car seat. This is not just a family rule. It is a law.
A *law* is a rule for everyone in a town, a state or a country. Leaders write laws. Police and judges help people follow them. Laws help keep people safe.
The United States has a big plan for its laws. It is called the *Constitution*. It was written in 1787. It still helps guide the country today.

words.d: a rule for everyone in a town, state or country
the main plan for the laws of the United States

look.title: Fair for Everyone
look.text: All are equal before the law and are entitled without any discrimination to equal protection of the law.
look.cite: United Nations, Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 7, 1948
look.prompt: This says the law is the same for all people. How is that like a fair rule at school?

check.q: What is a law?
choices: A rule for a whole town, state or country
check.why: A law is a rule for everyone in a town, state or country.

check.q: Which one is a law?
choices: Wear a seat belt in the car
check.why: Wearing a seat belt is a law. The others are home rules.

check.q: What is the main plan for laws in the United States?
check.why: The Constitution is the main plan for United States laws.

lessons.title: Rules in Other Countries
lessons.mainIdea: Every country has rules, and some are different from ours.
reading: In Chicago, cars drive on the right side of the road. In London, cars drive on the left side. In Tokyo, Japan, they drive on the left too.
Every country has rules and laws. Some rules are different. Some are the same. Children go to school in many countries. People stop at red lights almost everywhere.
When we visit a new place, we learn its rules. That is a kind and safe thing to do.

words.d: a land with its own people, leaders and laws

look.title: Shoes Off, Please
look.text: Mei visits her friend's home in Japan. At the door there is a low step. Shoes sit in a neat row. Mei takes off her shoes. She puts on soft slippers. Many homes in Japan have this custom.
look.prompt: Mei learned a rule in a new place. What did she do?

check.q: Which side of the road do cars use in London?
check.why: In London, cars drive on the left side of the road.

check.q: Do other countries have rules?
choices: No, only the United States does
check.why: The reading says every country has rules and laws.

check.q: What is a kind thing to do in a new place?
check.why: Learning the rules of a new place is kind and safe.

review.q: What does a rule tell us?
choices: What to do or not do
review.why: A rule tells us what to do or not do.

review.q: How did the tag game start again in the story?
choices: The children agreed on one rule
review.why: The children picked one rule together. Then the game worked.
A fair rule is the same for everyone.

review.q: What does green mean at a stoplight?
review.why: Green means go. Red means stop.

choices: A rule for a whole town, state or country
review.why: A law is a rule for everyone in a town, state or country.

review.q: You spill juice on a friend's paper. What helps?
choices: Say sorry and help clean up
review.why: We say sorry, help fix it and try again.

chapters.title: Leaders and Taking Turns
chapters.bigQuestion: How do leaders, voting and taking turns help a group get along?

story.title: A Name for the Fish
story.kicker: A class votes on a name for its new fish. Not everyone wins, but everyone helps.
paragraphs: Room 8 has a new fish. It is orange with a long tail. It swims in a round tank by the window. The fish needs a name. Everyone has an idea.
The teacher writes two names on the board: Sunny and Bubbles. "We will vote," she says. "Put up your hand for the name you like. The name with more hands wins."
Twelve hands go up for Sunny. Nine hands go up for Bubbles. Sunny wins! Carlos wanted Bubbles. He feels a little sad. That is okay. Feelings are okay.
The next day, it is Carlos's turn to feed the fish. He sprinkles the food. "Good morning, Sunny," he says. Sunny is the whole class's fish. Carlos still helps care for it.
story.think: Carlos did not get the name he wanted. Why did he still feed Sunny?

lessons.title: A Leader Helps a Group
lessons.mainIdea: A leader helps a group work together.
reading: The class goes on a walk to the park. Ms. Ruiz walks in front. She holds the line leader's hand. She checks that everyone is there. She keeps the group safe.
A *leader* helps a group. A leader listens. A leader helps the group choose. A leader helps everyone work together. A good leader cares about every person in the group.

words.d: a person who helps a group work together
some people who do things together

look.title: The Team Captain
look.text: Look at the soccer team. Nia is the captain today. She listens to her team. She says, "Let's pass more." She cheers when a friend kicks well. She helps a player who fell down.
look.prompt: What does Nia do that makes her a good leader?

check.q: What does a leader do?
check.why: A leader helps a group work together.

check.q: What does a good leader care about?
check.why: A good leader cares about every person in the group.

check.q: How did Ms. Ruiz help on the walk?
check.why: She checked that everyone was there and kept the group safe.

lessons.title: Mayors, Governors and Presidents
lessons.mainIdea: A mayor leads a city, a governor leads a state and a president leads a country.
reading: Chicago is a big city. It has a *mayor*. The mayor helps the city run. The mayor works on parks, buses and clean streets.
Illinois is a state. It has a *governor*. The governor leads the whole state. The United States is a country. It has a *president*. The president leads the whole country.
People vote to choose these leaders. The president serves four years at a time. Then the people vote again.

words.d: the leader of a city or town
the leader of a state
the leader of a country like the United States

look.title: How Long Leaders Serve
look.prompt: Which leader serves the longest before people vote again?

check.q: Who leads a city?
check.why: A mayor leads a city, like Chicago.

check.q: Who leads the state of Illinois?
check.why: A governor leads a state.

check.q: How many years does a president serve at a time?
check.why: The president serves four years. Then people vote again.

lessons.title: Kings, Queens and Emperors
lessons.mainIdea: Some countries have a king, queen or emperor as well as other leaders.
reading: The United Kingdom is a country far across the ocean. It has a *king*. His name is King Charles III. A king or queen often gets the job from their family.
Japan has an *emperor*. His name is Emperor Naruhito. In both countries, the king or emperor stands for the country. People also vote for other leaders who help make the laws.

words.d: a man who leads or stands for a country, often from a ruling family
the title for Japan's ruler who stands for the country

look.title: A Crown and a Vote
look.text: Picture two pictures side by side. In one, a king waves from a balcony in London. People cheer. In the other, a woman in London puts a paper in a vote box. Both show how the country works.
look.prompt: What is the same in both pictures? What is different?

check.q: Which country has a king named Charles III?
check.why: King Charles III is the king of the United Kingdom.

check.q: Japan has what kind of leader?
check.why: Japan has an emperor, Emperor Naruhito.

check.q: How does a king or queen often get the job?
check.why: A king or queen often gets the job from their family.

lessons.title: Voting to Choose
lessons.mainIdea: When we vote, each person gets one choice and the most votes win.
reading: The class wants a game for Friday. Some want tag. Some want freeze dance. How can they choose? They vote! Each child gets one vote.
A *vote* is how each person shows their choice. We count the votes. The choice with the most votes wins. Grown-ups vote for mayors, governors and presidents.
After a vote, we work together. We help, even if our choice did not win. Next time, our choice might win.

words.d: a way each person shows their choice

look.title: Everyone Takes Part
look.text: Everyone has the right to take part in the government of his country, directly or through freely chosen representatives.
look.cite: United Nations, Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 21, 1948
look.prompt: This says people can help choose their leaders. How do people do that?

check.q: How many votes does each child get?
check.why: Each person gets one vote. That is fair.

check.q: Which choice wins a vote?
choices: The one with the most votes
The one the loudest child likes
The one with the fewest votes
check.why: We count the votes. The most votes win.

check.q: What do we do after a vote?
choices: Work together, even if we lost
check.why: After a vote, we help and work together.

lessons.title: Taking Turns and Sharing
lessons.mainIdea: Taking turns and sharing let everyone have a fair chance.
reading: There is one red crayon. Two children want it. Ella uses it first. Then she hands it to Sam. They are *taking turns*.
Sharing means letting others use things too. When we take turns and share, everyone gets a chance. Nobody is left out. Groups get along better.

words.d: to go one at a time so everyone gets a chance
to let others use something too

look.title: The Block Tower
look.text: Look at the block corner. Three friends build one tall tower. Ava puts on a red block. Then Leo puts on a blue block. Then Kai puts on a green block. The tower grows and grows.
look.prompt: How are these friends taking turns?

check.q: What does it mean to take turns?
choices: To go one at a time
check.why: Taking turns means going one at a time so everyone gets a chance.

check.q: What did Ella do with the red crayon?
check.why: Ella used it first, then gave Sam a turn.

check.q: Why do we share?
check.why: Sharing lets everyone have a chance. Nobody is left out.

lessons.title: Jobs That Help Us All
lessons.mainIdea: Many people do jobs that help everyone.
reading: Before sunrise, a farmer picks apples. A bus driver starts the bus. A nurse checks on a sick baby. A teacher opens the classroom door.
Each of these jobs helps people. Farmers grow food. Nurses help people get well. Bus drivers take people where they need to go. Teachers help children learn. We need them all.

words.d: the work a person does
a person who helps care for sick people

look.title: A Day of Helpers
look.text: Think about your morning. You eat cereal. A farmer grew the grain. You ride the bus. A driver drives it. You go to school. A teacher says hello. Many people helped you before 9 o'clock!
look.prompt: Name two helpers you meet each day. What do they do?

check.q: What does a farmer do?
check.why: Farmers grow food for us to eat.

check.q: Who helps sick people get well?
check.why: Nurses help care for sick people.

check.q: Which jobs do we need?
check.why: The reading says each job helps people. We need them all.

lessons.title: Every Family Matters
lessons.mainIdea: Families with a lot of money and families with a little both matter the same.
reading: Some families have a lot of money. They may have a big house. Some families have a little money. They may share a small apartment. All of them love and care for each other.
Every person *matters*. Having more money does not make a person better. Having less does not make a person worse. We treat every family with the same respect.

words.d: to be important
treating someone as important and caring how they feel

look.title: Two Birthday Parties
look.text: Picture two parties. One is in a big backyard with a bounce house. One is in a small kitchen with one cake and paper hats. At both parties, a child blows out candles. Everyone sings. The child smiles.
look.prompt: What is the same about both parties?

check.q: Does having more money make a person better?
check.why: Money does not make a person better or worse. Every person matters.

check.q: What is respect?
check.why: Respect means treating someone as important and caring how they feel.

check.q: What do all the families in the reading do?
choices: Love and care for each other
check.why: Families with more money and less money all love and care for each other.

lessons.title: Kind to Everyone
lessons.mainIdea: We can be kind to people who look, talk or play differently from us.
reading: A new girl comes to class. Her name is Amira. She speaks Arabic at home. She is learning English. At lunch she sits alone.

Diego sits next to her. He smiles. He shows her his apple. She shows him her bread. They both laugh. Being *kind* means helping others feel welcome. Different is not wrong. Different is just different.

words.d: gentle and helpful to others
glad to have someone join you

look.title: Join the Game
look.text: Look at the playground. A boy uses a wheelchair. He watches a ball game. A girl rolls the ball to him. "Want to play?" she asks. He throws it back. Now the game has one more friend.
look.prompt: How did the girl help the boy feel welcome?

check.q: What did Diego do for Amira?
choices: He sat with her and smiled
check.why: Diego sat next to Amira and smiled. He helped her feel welcome.

check.q: What does kind mean?
check.why: Kind means gentle and helpful to others.

check.q: What does the reading say about being different?
check.why: The reading says different is not wrong. Different is just different.

review.q: In the story, why did Carlos feed Sunny?
choices: Sunny was the whole class's fish
review.why: Carlos lost the vote, but Sunny belongs to the whole class. He still helps.
A governor leads a state, like Illinois.
Japan has an emperor. The United Kingdom has a king.
We count the votes. The most votes win.

choices: So one person keeps it all
review.why: Taking turns gives everyone a fair chance.
Families with more or less money both matter the same.
